lessons.title: Context: Colonialism & Jacobean Power
lessons.description: Jacobean colonialism, New World exploration, masques, and Shakespeare’s late romances.
lessons.content_html:
Shakespeare’s World in 1611

The Tempest was written around 1610–1611, near the end of Shakespeare’s career. It is one of his final plays and belongs to a group known as the late romances. These plays share a pattern: older characters who have suffered loss find resolution through the younger generation, and the endings offer forgiveness rather than destruction. Understanding this context is essential for AQA’s AO3 — the play was shaped by the political anxieties, colonial ambitions, and theatrical fashions of Jacobean England.

Key Fact

The Tempest was almost certainly inspired by real events. In 1609, the ship Sea Venture, carrying colonists to Virginia, was wrecked in a storm off Bermuda. The survivors’ accounts — William Strachey’s True Reportory and Silvester Jourdain’s Discovery of the Bermudas — described a magical island of strange noises and abundant food. Shakespeare drew directly on these reports.

Colonialism and the New World

England in the early seventeenth century was gripped by excitement about the New World. The Virginia Company had established Jamestown in 1607, and investors were pouring money into colonial ventures. The relationship between European colonisers and indigenous peoples is central to The Tempest. Prospero arrives on an island already inhabited by Caliban, claims ownership of it, and forces Caliban into servitude. This mirrors the pattern of European colonisation: arrival, displacement, and exploitation.

Gonzalo’s speech in Act 2, Scene 1, where he imagines an ideal commonwealth with no property, work, or government, draws directly from Michel de Montaigne’s essay “Of Cannibals” (1580). Montaigne argued that supposedly “savage” peoples were morally superior to corrupt Europeans — an idea that Shakespeare both explores and complicates through Caliban.

Montaigne’s essay challenged European assumptions about civilisation. He argued that indigenous peoples lived in a natural state free from the corruption of European society. Gonzalo echoes this directly: “I’ th’ commonwealth I would by contraries / Execute all things.” He imagines no magistrates, no riches, no poverty. However, Shakespeare undercuts Gonzalo’s idealism — Antonio and Sebastian mock him throughout, and the play itself shows that even on a remote island, power struggles and treachery persist. The question of whether “civilisation” corrupts or improves people runs through the entire play.

The Jacobean Court and Masques

The Tempest was performed at court for King James I on 1 November 1611, and again in 1613 for the marriage of James’s daughter Princess Elizabeth. The play’s use of spectacle — the storm, Ariel’s transformations, the disappearing banquet, and the wedding masque in Act 4 — reflects the Jacobean fashion for lavish court masques. These were expensive entertainments that celebrated royal power through allegory and spectacle.

Prospero’s masque in Act 4 features the goddesses Iris, Ceres, and Juno blessing Ferdinand and Miranda’s marriage. This mirrors real masques performed for James I. But Prospero abruptly ends the masque when he remembers Caliban’s conspiracy, and his speech — “Our revels now are ended” — has been read as Shakespeare’s own farewell to the theatre. The masque-within-a-play structure creates layers of illusion: we watch an audience (Ferdinand and Miranda) watching a performance staged by a director (Prospero) within a play written by Shakespeare.

Key Fact

The Tempest was performed at the court of King James I in 1611. Act 4’s wedding masque with Iris, Ceres, and Juno directly mirrors the Jacobean court masque tradition. Prospero’s role as the director of spectacle on the island parallels Shakespeare’s own role as playwright — both create illusions that ultimately dissolve.

Power, Legitimacy, and Kingship

James I was deeply concerned with legitimate authority. He had written Basilikon Doron (1599) to instruct his son in the duties of kingship. The Tempest explores legitimate versus illegitimate power at every level: Prospero was overthrown by his brother Antonio; Antonio and Sebastian plot to murder Alonso; Caliban, Stephano, and Trinculo plot to murder Prospero. Every conspiracy in the play mirrors the others, suggesting that the desire to seize power by force is a universal human failing — not limited to any one class or race.

The late romances — Pericles, Cymbeline, The Winter’s Tale, and The Tempest — share key features: fathers separated from children, sea voyages, apparent loss followed by miraculous reunion, and endings that favour forgiveness over revenge. Unlike the tragedies (where flawed protagonists die), the romances allow their central figures a second chance. Prospero chooses mercy over vengeance: “The rarer action is / In virtue than in vengeance.” This pattern of reconciliation through the younger generation defines the genre.

For the exam, this generic context matters: The Tempest deliberately avoids tragedy. Prospero could destroy his enemies but chooses not to. This choice is the play’s moral centre, and it reflects the romance genre’s emphasis on restoration and renewal.

The Tempest is also notable for observing the classical unities of time, place, and action — the events unfold in roughly real time, on one island, with interconnected plotlines. This tight structure gives the play an unusual intensity and makes it feel like a carefully controlled experiment by Prospero (and by Shakespeare).
lessons.exam_tip_html: AO3 (context) is worth 4 of the 34 marks on the Shakespeare question, but embedding it well lifts your entire response. Do not write a standalone context paragraph. Instead, weave colonial and Jacobean references into your analysis: “Prospero’s enslavement of Caliban reflects the colonial mindset of Jacobean England, where indigenous peoples were routinely displaced and subjugated.” Always connect context to a specific quotation or moment in the text.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Tempest was inspired by the 1609 Sea Venture shipwreck and reflects Jacobean England’s fascination with New World colonisation — Prospero’s arrival on the island mirrors European colonial patterns.
  • The play was performed at King James I’s court in 1611; its masque sequences, spectacle, and themes of legitimate authority directly addressed Jacobean political concerns.
  • As a late romance, The Tempest favours forgiveness over revenge, with the older generation’s conflicts resolved through the younger generation’s love.

lessons.title: Act 1: The Storm & Prospero's Story
lessons.description: The storm, Prospero’s backstory, Ariel’s bond, and Caliban’s enslavement.
lessons.content_html:
Act 1, Scene 1: The Storm

The play opens with a violent tempest that threatens to sink a ship carrying Alonso (King of Naples), his son Ferdinand, Antonio (Prospero’s treacherous brother), Sebastian, Gonzalo, and others. The storm is significant because it immediately disrupts the normal social hierarchy: the Boatswain shouts at the nobles, telling them to stay out of the way: “What cares these roarers for the name of king?” The sea does not respect rank or title. This line establishes a key theme — the fragility of human authority when confronted by nature’s power.

Gonzalo, the honest old counsellor, tries to calm everyone: “The wills above be done! But I would fain die a dry death.” His characteristic mix of faith and dry humour marks him out from the start as the play’s moral compass. Meanwhile, the mariners struggle and Antonio curses. The scene is chaotic, noisy, and terrifying — and then we discover it was all staged by Prospero using magic.

Key Fact

The storm is artificial — created by Prospero through Ariel’s magic. No one is harmed, as Prospero later confirms: “Not a hair perished.” The key quotation “Hell is empty and all the devils are here” (spoken by Ferdinand in Ariel’s report) captures how terrifying the illusion was. It also foreshadows the play’s concern with the boundary between appearance and reality.

Act 1, Scene 2: Prospero’s Exposition

Scene 2 is the longest in the play and serves as a massive exposition dump. Prospero tells Miranda their history: he was the Duke of Milan, a scholar so absorbed in his books and magic that he neglected his duties and allowed his brother Antonio to seize power. Antonio conspired with Alonso, King of Naples, and Prospero and the infant Miranda were set adrift in “a rotten carcass of a butt” — a leaky boat. Only Gonzalo’s secret kindness, providing food, water, and Prospero’s beloved books, kept them alive.

Prospero’s telling is emotionally charged and controlling. He repeatedly interrupts himself to check Miranda is listening: “Dost thou attend me?” and “Thou attend’st not.” This reveals his need for control — even over the narrative of his own suffering. Miranda’s response is pure compassion: “O, I have suffered / With those that I saw suffer!” She feels others’ pain instinctively, establishing her as the play’s emotional heart.

Miranda has grown up on the island with no memory of Milan and no contact with other humans besides her father and Caliban. Her name means “admirable” or “wonderful” in Latin, and she lives up to it: she responds to the shipwreck with immediate empathy, not fear. Her famous line later in the play — “O brave new world, / That has such people in’t!” — is deeply ironic because the people she admires include the very men who betrayed her father. Her innocence is both her virtue and her vulnerability. Shakespeare uses her to ask whether goodness comes from nature or experience.

Ariel: The Bound Spirit

Ariel is an airy spirit who serves Prospero in exchange for a promise of freedom. Before Prospero arrived, Ariel had been imprisoned inside a “cloven pine” by the witch Sycorax for refusing to carry out her “earthy and abhorred commands.” Prospero freed Ariel but bound the spirit to his own service instead. When Ariel asks for liberty, Prospero responds with anger: “Dost thou forget / From what a torment I did free thee?”

This exchange is troubling. Prospero saved Ariel from one form of imprisonment only to impose another. He holds his act of rescue over Ariel as a permanent debt: “I must / Once in a month recount what thou hast been, / Which thou forget’st.” (actual line: Prospero must remind Ariel of her own history because Ariel tends to forget it — not that Ariel acknowledges a monthly debt to Prospero) The relationship is one of service, gratitude, and control. Ariel obeys, but always with one eye on the promised reward: freedom. Ariel’s yearning for liberty — “Do you love me, master?” — gives the character an emotional depth that goes beyond mere obedience.

Caliban: “This Island’s Mine”

Caliban is the most complex and debated character in the play. He is the son of Sycorax and the unnamed devil (described by Prospero as “the devil himself”). Setebos is the god that Sycorax worshipped — not Caliban’s father. When Prospero first arrived, Caliban and Prospero had a warm relationship: Caliban showed Prospero the island’s resources, and Prospero taught Caliban language. But after Caliban attempted to assault Miranda, Prospero enslaved him.

Caliban’s great speech of resentment makes his claim clear: “This island’s mine, by Sycorax my mother, / Which thou tak’st from me.” He articulates the experience of the dispossessed: “You taught me language, and my profit on’t / Is I know how to curse.” This is one of the play’s most powerful lines. Language — the supposed gift of civilisation — has only given Caliban the tools to express his rage at being subjugated. The coloniser’s “gift” becomes the colonised’s weapon.

Key Fact

“You taught me language, and my profit on’t / Is I know how to curse.” This quotation encapsulates the colonial dynamic: Prospero sees teaching language as a civilising gift, while Caliban sees it as a tool of oppression that only lets him articulate his suffering. The word “profit” is bitterly ironic — the only profit Caliban has gained from his colonisation is the ability to voice his dispossession.

In Act 1, Scene 2, Prospero uses magic to control every character: he creates the storm, puts Miranda to sleep, summons and threatens Ariel, and punishes Caliban with cramps. His magic is both a narrative device and a symbol of authority. It allows him to stage-manage every encounter on the island, from Ferdinand’s meeting with Miranda to the nobles’ wandering. But this control comes at a cost — it isolates him and prevents genuine human connection. The play’s resolution requires Prospero to renounce his magic and trust in human relationships instead.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For the AQA Shakespeare question, you must write about the extract AND the play as a whole. Act 1, Scene 2 is a likely extract choice because it contains so many key relationships. If you get an extract from this scene, identify whose relationship is being shown (Prospero–Miranda, Prospero–Ariel, or Prospero–Caliban), analyse the language closely for AO2, then zoom out to discuss how that relationship develops across the whole play. Use “Shakespeare presents…” to keep your focus on the writer’s craft.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The opening storm is artificial — Prospero’s magic controls nature and disrupts social hierarchy, establishing the play’s themes of power and illusion from the very first scene.
  • Caliban’s “You taught me language, and my profit on’t / Is I know how to curse” is the play’s most powerful statement about colonialism — the “gift” of civilisation becomes a weapon of resistance.
  • Prospero controls Ariel through obligation and Caliban through force; both relationships raise questions about the legitimacy and morality of power.

lessons.title: Acts 2-3: Power Struggles
lessons.description: Court conspiracies, Caliban’s rebellion, Ferdinand and Miranda, and the banquet.
lessons.content_html:
Act 2, Scene 1: The Court Party on the Island

After the shipwreck, the court party — Alonso, Sebastian, Antonio, Gonzalo, and others — find themselves scattered on the island. Alonso is grief-stricken, believing his son Ferdinand has drowned. Gonzalo tries to comfort him by noting the island’s beauty, but Antonio and Sebastian mock Gonzalo at every turn, their sardonic asides revealing their contempt for sincerity.

Gonzalo’s utopian speech imagines a commonwealth with “no sovereignty” — no king, no laws, no labour. Sebastian’s sneering response, “Yet he would be king on’t,” exposes the inherent contradiction: even a utopia needs someone to establish and maintain it. Shakespeare uses this moment to question whether any human society can truly exist without power structures. Gonzalo’s idealism is genuine but naïve; Antonio and Sebastian’s cynicism is perceptive but morally bankrupt.

Key Fact

When Ariel puts the court party to sleep (except Antonio and Sebastian), Antonio proposes murdering Alonso so that Sebastian can become King of Naples. This conspiracy directly mirrors Antonio’s earlier usurpation of Prospero — Shakespeare creates a structural parallel showing that Antonio has learned nothing and will always reach for illegitimate power. Ariel wakes Gonzalo just in time to prevent the assassination.

Antonio: The Unrepentant Villain

Antonio is the play’s most purely villainous character. Unlike Macbeth or Claudius, he shows no guilt, no hesitation, and no internal conflict. When he tempts Sebastian to murder Alonso, his language is chillingly pragmatic: “What’s past is prologue” — the past is merely the introduction to what comes next. He treats the murder of a king as a simple strategic move. His influence over Sebastian mirrors his earlier corruption of Milan’s political order when he overthrew Prospero.

Crucially, Antonio never apologises at the end of the play. When Prospero forgives him, Antonio says nothing. This silence is one of the most debated moments in The Tempest — does it suggest shame, defiance, or simply an inability to change? Shakespeare leaves it unresolved, refusing to give the audience the comfort of a complete moral transformation.

The Tempest contains three overlapping conspiracies against authority: Antonio’s past usurpation of Prospero in Milan, Antonio and Sebastian’s plot to murder Alonso on the island, and Caliban’s alliance with Stephano and Trinculo to murder Prospero. Each conspiracy reflects a different social level — aristocratic, political, and servant-class — but they all share the same structure: a tempter corrupts a willing follower. Shakespeare suggests that the desire to seize power by treachery is a universal human flaw, not confined to any one class.

Act 2, Scene 2 & Act 3, Scene 2: Caliban, Stephano, and Trinculo

The subplot involving Caliban, Stephano (a drunken butler), and Trinculo (a jester) provides comic relief but also serious thematic weight. When Caliban encounters Stephano and his wine, he mistakes the drunkard for a god: “That’s a brave god, and bears celestial liquor.” He immediately offers himself as Stephano’s servant: “I’ll show thee every fertile inch o’ th’ island … I prithee, let me bring thee where crabs grow.”

This mirrors exactly what Caliban did when Prospero first arrived. He is repeating the cycle of colonisation: offering his knowledge of the island to a new master in the hope of escaping the old one. Shakespeare shows that Caliban’s desire for freedom leads him into a new form of subjugation. Yet Caliban’s speech about the island — “Be not afeard; the isle is full of noises, / Sounds and sweet airs, that give delight and hurt not” — is some of the most beautiful poetry in the play, revealing a sensitivity that neither Stephano nor Trinculo possess.

Key Fact

“Be not afeard; the isle is full of noises, / Sounds and sweet airs, that give delight and hurt not.” This speech (Act 3, Scene 2) reveals Caliban’s deep emotional connection to the island. His language here is lyrical and gentle — entirely different from his angry exchanges with Prospero. Shakespeare uses this contrast to show that Caliban is not simply a “monster” but a complex being with an inner life that his oppressors cannot see or value.

Act 3, Scene 1: Ferdinand and Miranda

Prospero has set Ferdinand to the menial task of carrying logs — a test of his love for Miranda. Ferdinand accepts willingly: “The mistress which I serve quickens what’s dead.” His language of willing servitude contrasts sharply with Caliban’s forced labour and Ariel’s bound service. Ferdinand chooses to serve out of love, while Caliban and Ariel serve out of compulsion. Shakespeare draws a clear distinction between willing service and slavery.

Miranda offers to carry the logs for Ferdinand, breaking her father’s instructions. She even tells Ferdinand her name despite Prospero’s explicit command not to. Their exchange is sincere and direct: “I am your wife, if you will marry me; / If not, I’ll die your maid.” Miranda’s boldness subverts the typical Jacobean expectation that women should be passive. Prospero watches in secret, pleased: his plan is working. The love match will unite Milan and Naples, restoring political order through the younger generation.

Act 3, Scene 3: The Vanishing Banquet

Prospero stages a spectacular illusion: spirits present a lavish banquet to the hungry court party, then Ariel appears as a harpy and makes it vanish. Ariel denounces Alonso, Antonio, and Sebastian as “three men of sin” who overthrew Prospero: “The powers, delaying, not forgetting, have / Incensed the seas and shores — yea, all the creatures — / Against your peace.” The vanishing banquet symbolises how the material rewards of treachery are ultimately empty. Alonso is moved to guilt and despair; Antonio and Sebastian draw their swords uselessly against spirits they cannot fight.

A harpy in classical mythology is a creature of divine vengeance that snatches food from the guilty. By having Ariel appear in this form, Shakespeare frames Prospero’s justice as divinely sanctioned. The banquet scene is also a masque-like spectacle that demonstrates Prospero’s absolute control over the island. The “three men of sin” are powerless against his magic. Yet this scene also raises the question: is Prospero dispensing justice or enacting revenge? The line between the two is deliberately blurred.

  • Three conspiracies — Antonio’s past usurpation, the plot against Alonso, and Caliban’s rebellion — structurally mirror each other, showing the universal human desire to seize power by treachery.
  • Caliban’s “Be not afeard; the isle is full of noises” is some of the play’s most beautiful poetry, revealing a sensitivity that challenges the label of “monster” and complicates the colonial reading.
  • Ferdinand’s willing service out of love contrasts with Caliban’s forced labour and Ariel’s bound service, drawing a key distinction between love and slavery.

lessons.title: Acts 4-5: Resolution & Forgiveness
lessons.description: The masque, ‘Our revels’ speech, forgiveness, renouncing magic, and the epilogue.
lessons.content_html:
Act 4, Scene 1: The Wedding Masque

Prospero has tested Ferdinand’s love through the log-carrying task and is now satisfied. He blesses the marriage between Ferdinand and Miranda, and stages an elaborate masque performed by spirits. The goddesses Iris, Ceres, and Juno descend to bless the couple with fertility, abundance, and a prosperous future. The masque is beautiful, orderly, and controlled — a vision of harmony that represents everything Prospero hopes to achieve through his plan.

But Prospero abruptly stops the masque when he remembers Caliban’s conspiracy. The spirits vanish, and Ferdinand and Miranda are startled. Prospero’s fury reveals that his control is not as absolute as it appears — the messy reality of human treachery disrupts even his most carefully staged illusion. This interruption is structurally significant: it shatters the artificial perfection of the masque and forces Prospero to confront the world as it really is, not as he would design it.

Key Fact

Prospero’s speech after dismissing the masque is one of Shakespeare’s most famous passages: “Our revels now are ended. These our actors, / As I foretold you, were all spirits and / Are melted into air, into thin air.” He extends the metaphor to all of human existence: “The cloud-capped towers, the gorgeous palaces, / The solemn temples, the great globe itself … shall dissolve.” “The great globe” is simultaneously the world and Shakespeare’s own theatre (the Globe). The speech works on three levels: the masque has ended, all life is temporary, and theatre itself is an illusion.

“We Are Such Stuff as Dreams Are Made On”

The full line reads: “We are such stuff / As dreams are made on, and our little life / Is rounded with a sleep.” This is a metatheatrical moment: Prospero is both a character addressing Ferdinand and a playwright addressing the audience. The word “rounded” means both “completed” and “surrounded” — our lives are brief episodes enclosed by oblivion, just as a play is enclosed by darkness before the curtain rises and after it falls.

For the exam , this speech is crucial because it connects three of the play’s major themes: the nature of illusion, the transience of power, and Shakespeare’s self-reflexive exploration of his own art. If you are given an extract from Act 4 or asked about the theme of illusion, this speech should be at the centre of your response.

Prospero defeats Caliban, Stephano, and Trinculo not through violence but through distraction. He sets out “glistering apparel” — fine clothes — which Stephano and Trinculo cannot resist stealing, despite Caliban’s desperate pleas to focus on the murder plot. Prospero then sets spirits in the shape of dogs to chase them away. The scene is comic, but it makes a serious point: Stephano and Trinculo are easily corrupted by the trappings of wealth and status, exposing the hollowness of their rebellion. Caliban is the only one with genuine grievances, yet he has chosen the worst possible allies.

Act 5, Scene 1: “The Rarer Action Is in Virtue”

Act 5 is the play’s moral climax. Ariel reports that the imprisoned nobles are suffering — Gonzalo is weeping, and Alonso, Antonio, and Sebastian are distracted with grief and madness. Ariel adds a remarkable line: “Your charm so strongly works ’em / That if you now beheld them, your affections / Would become tender … Mine would, sir, were I human.” The spirit who is not human feels more compassion than the human characters who wronged Prospero.

Prospero is moved: “Hast thou, which art but air, a touch, a feeling / Of their afflictions, and shall not myself … be kindlier moved than thou art?” He makes the defining choice of the play: “The rarer action is / In virtue than in vengeance.” Revenge is common; mercy is rare and difficult. This single decision transforms the play from potential tragedy into romance. Prospero chooses to be better than his enemies.

Key Fact

“The rarer action is / In virtue than in vengeance.” Prospero chooses mercy over revenge, prompted by Ariel’s compassion. This is the play’s turning point: it transforms the ending from punishment to reconciliation. The word “rarer” acknowledges that forgiveness is harder and less natural than revenge — making it the more admirable (“virtuous”) choice.

Renouncing Magic: “I’ll Break My Staff”

Before confronting the nobles, Prospero delivers his great renunciation speech: “I have bedimmed / The noontide sun, called forth the mutinous winds … But this rough magic / I here abjure.” He lists his magical achievements, then rejects them. He promises: “I’ll break my staff, / Bury it certain fathoms in the earth, / And deeper than did ever plummet sound / I’ll drown my book.”

The staff and the book are his sources of power. By destroying them, Prospero surrenders his ability to control others. This is a renunciation that works on multiple levels: the character abandons magic, the playwright (Shakespeare) abandons his art, and the authority figure surrenders the tools of domination. Prospero will face the world as an ordinary man — “Now my charms are all o’erthrown, / And what strength I have’s mine own, / Which is most faint.”

Forgiveness and Its Limits

Prospero forgives Alonso, who is genuinely repentant and overjoyed to find Ferdinand alive. He forgives Gonzalo warmly. But his “forgiveness” of Antonio is much colder: “For you, most wicked sir, whom to call brother / Would even infect my mouth, I do forgive / Thy rankest fault.” The language is hostile even as the words are merciful. And Antonio, crucially, says nothing in response — no apology, no gratitude, no acknowledgement.

Prospero’s acknowledgement of Caliban is equally ambiguous: “This thing of darkness I / Acknowledge mine.” On one level, he takes responsibility for Caliban. On another, he claims ownership. The line can be read as an admission of guilt (“I created this situation”), a recognition of his own capacity for darkness, or simply a statement of possession. Shakespeare leaves the interpretation open.

The epilogue is unique in Shakespeare. Prospero steps forward alone and addresses the audience directly: “Now my charms are all o’erthrown, / And what strength I have’s mine own.” He has given up his magic and now depends entirely on the audience’s goodwill. He asks to be “set free” by their applause: “As you from crimes would pardoned be, / Let your indulgence set me free.” The word “indulgence” carries a religious echo — a pardon for sins. Prospero (and Shakespeare) asks the audience to extend the same mercy the play has preached. The power dynamic reverses completely: the master magician is now a supplicant, powerless without the audience’s approval.

If you get either, analyse the metatheatrical layer: Prospero as playwright, the masque as play-within-a-play, the staff and book as symbols of creative/magical power. For AO2, explore the extended metaphor of life-as-dream and the imagery of dissolution. For AO3, link to Shakespeare’s own retirement from the stage.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • “Our revels now are ended” and “We are such stuff as dreams are made on” work on three levels: the masque ending, all life being temporary, and Shakespeare’s farewell to theatre.
  • “The rarer action is / In virtue than in vengeance” is the play’s moral turning point — Prospero chooses mercy over revenge, prompted by Ariel’s compassion.
  • Prospero’s renunciation of his staff and book symbolises the surrender of power, while “This thing of darkness I acknowledge mine” remains deliberately ambiguous.

lessons.title: Character Analysis
lessons.description: Deep analysis of Prospero, Caliban, Ariel, Miranda, Antonio, Ferdinand, and Gonzalo.
lessons.content_html:
Prospero: The Magician-Duke

Prospero is the play’s protagonist, antagonist, director, and moral centre all at once. He is a contradictory figure: a wronged duke who deserves justice, but also an authoritarian who enslaves Caliban, binds Ariel, controls Miranda’s marriage, and manipulates everyone on the island. His magic gives him god-like power, yet he is driven by very human emotions — bitterness, anger, and eventually compassion.

Shakespeare presents Prospero as a figure who must learn to let go. In Milan, he was too absorbed in books and magic, allowing Antonio to seize power. On the island, he becomes obsessed with control — staging every encounter, punishing disobedience, and choreographing the reunion. His growth comes when Ariel’s compassion shames him into choosing “virtue” over “vengeance.” By breaking his staff and drowning his book, he surrenders the tools that define him. In the epilogue, stripped of magic, he is vulnerable: “Now my charms are all o’erthrown, / And what strength I have’s mine own, / Which is most faint.”

Key Fact

Prospero’s character arc moves from control to surrender. He creates the storm, puts Miranda to sleep, binds Ariel with threats, enslaves Caliban, orchestrates the Ferdinand–Miranda meeting, stages the masque, and traps his enemies. His decision to forgive and renounce magic is not easy — the word “rarer” acknowledges this. For AO1, track how his relationship with power changes across the play.

Caliban: Monster, Victim, Poet

Caliban is the most debated character in the play. Prospero and Miranda call him a “thing of darkness,” a “monster,” and “a born devil.” These labels define how the colonial master sees the colonised subject. But Shakespeare gives Caliban some of the play’s most beautiful and eloquent language: “Be not afeard; the isle is full of noises, / Sounds and sweet airs, that give delight and hurt not.” This poetry reveals an interior life that contradicts the “monster” label entirely.

Caliban’s claim to the island is presented as legitimate: “This island’s mine, by Sycorax my mother, / Which thou tak’st from me.” He has been dispossessed by Prospero’s arrival. His line “You taught me language, and my profit on’t / Is I know how to curse” encapsulates the colonial dynamic: the coloniser’s “gift” becomes the weapon the colonised turns against them. Yet Caliban’s attempted assault on Miranda complicates any simple reading of him as a noble victim. Shakespeare refuses to simplify him.

Post-colonial critics have recast Caliban as the play’s true hero — the indigenous inhabitant whose land and culture are stolen by a European coloniser. Aimé Césaire’s A Tempest (1969) rewrites the play from Caliban’s perspective, making him a symbol of anti-colonial resistance. In this reading, Caliban’s “curses” are acts of resistance, his knowledge of the island represents indigenous wisdom that the coloniser exploits, and Prospero’s “civilising” mission is a cover for domination. For AO3, this contextual lens can transform your analysis of every Caliban scene.

Ariel: Spirit, Servant, Conscience

Ariel is a spirit of the air who longs for freedom. Unlike Caliban, Ariel serves Prospero willingly (if not happily), performing every task with skill and even artistry. Ariel creates the storm, leads Ferdinand to Miranda with a song, appears as a harpy to terrify the nobles, and stages the wedding masque. Ariel’s shapeshifting reflects the protean nature of theatrical performance itself.

Ariel’s most significant moment comes in Act 5, when the spirit describes the nobles’ suffering and adds: “Mine [affections] would [become tender], sir, were I human.” This is the play’s emotional pivot. A non-human creature expresses more compassion than Prospero himself, shaming the magician into mercy. Ariel functions as Prospero’s conscience — the voice that reminds him what humanity should mean, even though Ariel is not human.

Miranda: Innocence and Agency

Miranda has grown up in isolation, knowing only Prospero and Caliban. Her response to the world is defined by wonder and empathy: “O, I have suffered / With those that I saw suffer!” and later, “O brave new world, / That has such people in’t!” (The latter is bitterly ironic, since the “brave new world” includes Antonio and Sebastian.) Miranda is often read as a passive figure controlled by her father, but she shows real agency: she defies Prospero by telling Ferdinand her name, offers to carry his logs, and proposes marriage herself.

Antonio, Ferdinand, and Gonzalo

Antonio is the play’s unreformed villain. He usurped Prospero, plots to murder Alonso, and never apologises or shows remorse. His silence at the end is one of the play’s most troubling moments — forgiveness is offered but never accepted. Antonio represents the limit of Prospero’s power: magic can compel obedience but cannot force genuine repentance.

Ferdinand serves as a foil to Caliban. Both serve Prospero, but Ferdinand serves willingly out of love, while Caliban serves under compulsion. Ferdinand’s willingness to carry logs proves his worth and allows the dynastic marriage that resolves the political conflict. He is honourable but relatively straightforward — his function is structural rather than psychological.

Gonzalo is the play’s moral compass. He saved Prospero and Miranda with food, water, and books. His utopian vision in Act 2 reflects genuine idealism, even if Antonio and Sebastian mock it. Prospero’s first acknowledgement in Act 5 is to Gonzalo: “Holy Gonzalo, honourable man.” Gonzalo represents the possibility that goodness can survive in a corrupt world.

Shakespeare structures the characters as foils. Ferdinand’s willing service contrasts Caliban’s enslavement. Gonzalo’s honesty contrasts Antonio’s treachery. Ariel’s obedient service contrasts Caliban’s rebellion. Miranda’s innocence contrasts Antonio’s corruption. These contrasts are deliberate: they force the audience to ask whether goodness is innate (nature) or learned (nurture) — a question Shakespeare never definitively answers.

Key Fact

The play’s characters are structured as foils: Ferdinand (love) vs Caliban (force), Gonzalo (loyalty) vs Antonio (betrayal), Ariel (spirit-obedience) vs Caliban (physical-rebellion). These contrasts test whether goodness is innate or shaped by experience — the nature vs nurture debate that runs through the entire play.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When analysing characters for AQA, always discuss how Shakespeare presents them — through language, imagery, structural position, and what other characters say about them. For Caliban, contrast what Prospero calls him (“thing of darkness,” “monster”) with what he says himself (“Be not afeard; the isle is full of noises”). This gap between reputation and reality is where the best AO2 analysis lives. Always use “Shakespeare presents…” not “Caliban is…”
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Prospero is contradictory: a wronged duke who deserves justice but also an authoritarian controller. His arc moves from absolute power to voluntary surrender.
  • Caliban is monster, victim, and poet simultaneously — Shakespeare refuses to simplify him. Post-colonial readings recast him as the play’s true protagonist.
  • The characters function as foils: Ferdinand vs Caliban (willing vs forced service), Gonzalo vs Antonio (honesty vs treachery), Ariel vs Caliban (obedience vs rebellion).

lessons.title: Colonialism, Magic & Structure
lessons.description: Post-colonial readings, magic as art, the classical unities, and the epilogue.
lessons.content_html:
Colonialism: Prospero as Coloniser

The most influential modern reading of The Tempest interprets the play through the lens of post-colonialism. In this reading, Prospero is the European coloniser: he arrives on an island already inhabited by Caliban, claims ownership, imposes his language and culture, and forces the native into servitude. Caliban’s resentment — “This island’s mine, by Sycorax my mother, / Which thou tak’st from me” — is the cry of every dispossessed indigenous people under European empire.

The parallels with Jacobean colonialism are striking. England was actively colonising the New World when Shakespeare wrote the play. The Virginia Company had established Jamestown in 1607, and the Sea Venture shipwreck of 1609 provided direct source material. Prospero’s treatment of Caliban mirrors the colonial pattern: initial cooperation (“When thou cam’st first, / Thou strok’dst me and made much of me”), followed by exploitation, forced labour, and cultural erasure.

Key Fact

“You taught me language, and my profit on’t / Is I know how to curse.” This line is central to post-colonial readings. The coloniser’s “gift” of language was intended to “civilise” Caliban, but he uses it to resist. The bitter irony of “profit” — a word drawn from the commercial vocabulary of colonialism — exposes the transaction: Prospero expected gratitude and obedience in return for education, but Caliban refuses to play the grateful native.

Martinican writer Aimé Césaire adapted The Tempest as A Tempest, explicitly framing Caliban as a Black slave resisting a white coloniser. In Césaire’s version, Caliban rejects his coloniser’s name entirely: “Call me X.” This allusion to Malcolm X transforms the play into a direct statement about racial decolonisation. While you should not treat Césaire’s version as identical to Shakespeare’s, knowing that this reading exists demonstrates sophisticated contextual understanding (AO3). It shows the examiner that you can see the play from multiple perspectives.

Magic as Art and Theatre

Prospero’s magic can be read as an allegory for Shakespeare’s art. Both Prospero and Shakespeare create illusions that move, terrify, and delight audiences. Prospero stages the storm, the masque, the harpy banquet, and the spirits — all of which are theatrical spectacles. His famous line, “Our revels now are ended,” is widely read as Shakespeare’s own farewell to the stage. When Prospero breaks his staff and drowns his book, it mirrors the playwright laying down his pen.

This metatheatrical reading transforms every use of magic in the play into a commentary on the power and limitations of art. Prospero can create stunning illusions, but he cannot force genuine repentance (Antonio never apologises). Art can move people emotionally, but it cannot change their fundamental nature. In the epilogue, Prospero acknowledges this: stripped of his theatrical magic, he depends on the audience’s “indulgence” — their willingness to be moved.

The Unities: Time, Place, and Action

The Tempest is Shakespeare’s most structurally disciplined play. It observes the three classical unities: the action takes place on one island (place), within approximately three hours of real time (time), and follows a single overarching plan orchestrated by Prospero (action). Prospero himself draws attention to this: “What is the time o’ th’ day? … The time ’twixt six and now / Must by us both be spent most preciously.”

The tight structure creates a sense of controlled intensity that mirrors Prospero’s own orchestration. Everything on the island happens according to his design — the characters are moved around like actors hitting their marks. This structural choice reinforces the metatheatrical reading: the island is a stage, Prospero is the director, and the other characters are performers in a play they do not know they are in. For AO2, the unities are a structural feature you can analyse to show how form reflects meaning.

The epilogue is spoken directly to the audience by Prospero alone. He has renounced his magic and freed Ariel; now he asks to be freed himself by the audience’s applause. “Now my charms are all o’erthrown, / And what strength I have’s mine own, / Which is most faint.” The epilogue operates simultaneously as a character’s plea, an actor’s curtain call, and a playwright’s farewell. The final couplet — “As you from crimes would pardoned be, / Let your indulgence set me free” — invokes the Lord’s Prayer (“Forgive us our trespasses, as we forgive those who trespass against us”). The audience becomes the final authority: they hold the power to release or condemn.

Key Fact

The Tempest’s structure reinforces its themes. The unities of time, place, and action mirror Prospero’s absolute control. The masque-within-a-play is a performance within a performance within a performance. The epilogue breaks the fourth wall, collapsing the boundary between Prospero’s magic and Shakespeare’s theatre. Form and content are inseparable — the play’s structure is its meaning.

Nature Versus Nurture

Prospero calls Caliban “A devil, a born devil, on whose nature / Nurture can never stick.” This is the clearest statement of the nature versus nurture debate in the play. Prospero believes Caliban is inherently evil and that education (“nurture”) has failed. But the play complicates this position: Caliban’s beautiful poetry suggests an inner sensitivity that contradicts the “born devil” label, and the fact that Antonio — a European noble raised with every civilising advantage — is equally treacherous undermines Prospero’s claim that only Caliban is irredeemable by nature.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For AO3, you do not need to write a separate paragraph about colonialism or metatheatre. Instead, embed these readings into your language analysis. For example: “Caliban’s use of the commercial term ‘profit’ reflects the transactional logic of colonialism — Prospero expected obedience as payment for education, mirroring the Jacobean colonial assumption that indigenous peoples should be grateful for European ‘civilisation.’” This integrates context (AO3) with language analysis (AO2) in a single sentence.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Post-colonial readings recast Prospero as a coloniser and Caliban as the dispossessed native. Caliban’s “I know how to curse” turns the coloniser’s “gift” into a weapon of resistance.
  • Prospero’s magic allegorically represents Shakespeare’s art: both create powerful illusions but cannot force genuine change. The epilogue completes this parallel.
  • The classical unities of time, place, and action mirror Prospero’s controlled orchestration of events, reinforcing the metatheatrical dimension where form reflects meaning.

lessons.title: Key Themes & Exam Technique
lessons.description: Five key themes with quotations and AQA extract-and-essay technique.
lessons.content_html:
Theme 1: Power and Control

Power is the spine of The Tempest. Every character either holds power, seeks it, or suffers under it. Prospero’s legitimate claim to the dukedom was stolen by Antonio’s treachery, and the play is structured around Prospero’s attempt to restore what was taken from him. But Shakespeare complicates this: in reclaiming his power, Prospero enslaves Caliban, binds Ariel, and controls Miranda’s marriage — using the same domination he condemns in Antonio.

The three conspiracies (Antonio’s usurpation, Antonio and Sebastian’s plot against Alonso, Caliban’s plot against Prospero) show that the desire for illegitimate power operates at every level of society. Even Stephano, a drunken butler, immediately begins fantasising about ruling the island. Shakespeare suggests that power corrupts universally, and that the difference between a legitimate ruler and a tyrant may be a matter of perspective rather than principle.

Key Fact

Key quotations for power: “What cares these roarers for the name of king?” (nature strips away authority), “I’ll break my staff” (voluntary surrender of power), “This island’s mine” (colonised claiming ownership), “What’s past is prologue” (power seized without guilt). The play asks whether any form of power can be truly legitimate.

Theme 2: Freedom and Slavery

Freedom is what every character wants. Ariel longs for liberty: “Do you love me, master? … I prithee … my liberty.” Caliban seeks freedom from Prospero’s enslavement. Ferdinand willingly accepts temporary bondage (carrying logs) to earn Miranda’s hand. Prospero himself is trapped on the island by his need for revenge — he can only leave when he lets go of his resentment.

Shakespeare creates a spectrum of servitude. Ferdinand’s willing service through love occupies one end; Caliban’s forced labour under threat of cramps occupies the other; Ariel’s conditional service (freedom promised in exchange for obedience) sits in between. The play suggests that true freedom requires not just release from bondage but a change in the power-holder’s heart. Prospero must choose to free Ariel and forgive his enemies — no one forces him. His own freedom depends on his capacity for mercy.

In the epilogue, Prospero asks the audience: “Let your indulgence set me free.” The master who controlled everyone on the island is now dependent on others for his own release. This reversal completes the play’s exploration of freedom: everyone is bound to someone else, and liberation is an act of grace, not strength. The word “indulgence” carries both a theatrical meaning (applause) and a religious one (a pardon for sins), connecting the theme of freedom to the theme of forgiveness.

Theme 3: Forgiveness and Reconciliation

Reconciliation is the romance genre’s signature theme. Unlike tragedy, where the protagonist is destroyed, the late romances allow for second chances. Prospero’s choice — “The rarer action is / In virtue than in vengeance” — defines the play’s moral centre. But Shakespeare does not present forgiveness as easy or complete. Prospero’s words to Antonio are bitter: “For you, most wicked sir, whom to call brother / Would even infect my mouth.” Antonio never responds. The play’s forgiveness is imperfect, conditional, and uncertain — which makes it more realistic and more dramatically interesting than a simple happy ending.

Key Fact

Forgiveness operates on three levels in Act 5: Alonso is genuinely forgiven (he repents, and Ferdinand’s survival brings reconciliation); Antonio is coldly forgiven (Prospero’s language remains hostile, and Antonio never apologises); Caliban is ambiguously acknowledged (“This thing of darkness I acknowledge mine”). This spectrum shows that forgiveness is not a single act but a complex, imperfect process.

Theme 4: Art, Illusion, and Reality

The entire play is an illusion created by Prospero, who is himself a character in an illusion created by Shakespeare. The storm is artificial. The masque dissolves. The banquet vanishes. Even Ariel’s music is designed to manipulate emotions. “We are such stuff / As dreams are made on, and our little life / Is rounded with a sleep” extends the metaphor to all existence: everything — power, revenge, love, theatre — is temporary and constructed. Shakespeare uses the play to meditate on the power and fragility of his own art.

Theme 5: Nature Versus Nurture

Prospero declares Caliban “A devil, a born devil, on whose nature / Nurture can never stick.” But the play provides counter-evidence: Caliban’s sensitive poetry, his genuine love for the island, and the fact that Antonio — raised with every privilege — is equally treacherous. Miranda, raised in isolation with only nature and one teacher, develops into a compassionate person. Ferdinand proves his worth through character, not breeding. Shakespeare asks whether people are shaped by their birth (“nature”) or their experience (“nurture”), and deliberately refuses to answer.

Shakespeare questions typically provide a short printed extract and ask you to explore a theme, character or idea both in the extract and across the play as a whole. Plan your time so you give real attention to both halves — candidates who treat the extract as an afterthought, or who never return to it, tend to miss marks. Check your exam board’s specimen paper for exact timing and wording.

What the assessment objectives reward: AO1 is an informed, personal response supported by well-chosen textual references; AO2 is analysis of how Shakespeare uses language, form and structure to create meanings and effects; AO3 is understanding of the relationship between the play and its contexts; AO4 is accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar. In a Shakespeare essay, close language and structural analysis tied to a clear personal argument carry the most weight. Context matters, but it supports analysis rather than standing alone — weave it throughout rather than writing a separate paragraph.

Exam Technique: Structuring Your Response

A strong response has roughly this shape: begin with the extract (2–3 paragraphs of close analysis), then move to the play as a whole (2–3 paragraphs), weaving context throughout rather than adding it as a separate section. Each paragraph should follow the pattern: point → quotation → word-level analysis → contextual link → effect on audience. For example:

“Shakespeare presents Caliban as a multifaceted character through his claim ‘This island’s mine, by Sycorax my mother.’ The possessive ‘mine’ and the legal grounding ‘by Sycorax my mother’ establish a legitimate ownership claim that mirrors the land rights of indigenous peoples displaced by European colonisers. A Jacobean audience might have dismissed Caliban’s claim, but a modern audience recognises the colonial injustice Shakespeare encodes here.” This single paragraph draws together personal argument, close language analysis and contextual understanding.

Key Fact

Priorities in a Shakespeare essay: a clear personal argument backed by precise textual evidence (AO1); close analysis of language, form and structure and the effects Shakespeare creates (AO2); context woven through rather than bolted on (AO3); and accurate written expression (AO4). Close analysis of language, tied to an argued response, is the heart of the mark scheme. Check your exam board’s specimen paper for the exact mark weightings.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Learn 10–12 key quotations across the five themes (power, freedom, forgiveness, nature vs nurture, illusion) and practise using each one in multiple contexts. A quotation like “This thing of darkness I acknowledge mine” can answer questions about colonialism, forgiveness, power, or character. Flexibility with quotations is more valuable than memorising many — depth of analysis beats breadth of evidence every time.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The five key themes — power, freedom, forgiveness, nature vs nurture, and illusion — are interconnected: Prospero must surrender power, grant freedom, choose forgiveness, accept human nature’s complexity, and release his illusions.
  • For AQA, AO1 + AO2 (response + language analysis) are worth 24 of 34 marks. Close analysis of individual words and images is far more important than listing contextual facts.
  • Structure your essay: extract first (close analysis), then the play as a whole, with context embedded throughout using the point → quotation → analysis → context → effect pattern.
